chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 481 to 490, Peyanar's mullai decade of the man bidding his chariot home (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து): his work for the king done and the rains come, the returning husband urges his charioteer to goad the bird-swift horses and drive fast, so that his waiting wife's pining may end, her beauty return and her heart rejoice at the evening hour.

481.reading: Thinking of the woman of red jewels, with shoulders like bamboo sloping at the joint and a lovely lined waist, the man tells his charioteer to put the goad to the bird-swift proud horses yoked to his chariot and drive, so that the sickness may leave.
481.nuance: The goad (முள், a thorn) is asked for outright: the horses are to be hurt so that a sickness ends, and the poem does not say whose sickness (நோய்), his longing or hers, so the one cure serves both. The image of the horses as birds returns word for word in 486.

thinai_evidence.note: the man, thinking of his wife, hurries home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 3

comparisons.tenor: a day's further delay with the king

482.reading: Drive very fast, charioteer, so that I come as a great guest to the woman of chosen jewels: to stay even one day more with the king whose white-speared army wins and slays would be longer than an age.
482.nuance: The man names himself the feast (பெருவிருந்து) he will be for his wife, turning the duty of the house to receive guests into the joy of his own return. The king's victory is granted in one line and then measured against a single day, which becomes an aeon (ஊழி): royal service is honoured only as long as it lasts.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's war is done and the man hastens home to his waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; பாக, line 2

483.reading: The roads have spread with blossom and grown lovely, the king has let us go, the horses are racing; drive on ahead, charioteer, so that the woman of fair brow may have her beauty back.
483.nuance: Three short clauses, each closed with ஏ, give the release in steps: the season, the king, the horses, and only then the order. Her beauty (தன்னலம்) is what separation took and what his arrival restores, so the drive is a cure for her body as much as a homecoming.

thinai_evidence.note: released by the king, the man hurries to the waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; பாக, line 3

484.reading: Summer has gone, the rain clouds have poured, the forest has taken on its beauty and the season is at its full; drive swiftly, charioteer, for we have stayed far too long, forgetting her of fine jewels.
484.nuance: The man accuses himself: மறந்தே, 'having forgotten', is the charge an abandoned wife makes, here in the husband's own mouth. பாடுசிறந்து may be the swelling sound of the rain or the season reaching its height; either way the land's fullness is the measure of his delay.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come and the forest has grown lovely

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; பாக, line 3

485.reading: So that her hard pining grief may end and I may embrace her great shoulders as their beauty comes back, drive the chariot, charioteer, across the flower-decked scrub where the deer leap startled.
485.nuance: அவளும் ... யாமும் sets two griefs side by side: her pining ends and his embrace begins, so the return is said to be needed by both. ஏமதி வலவ தேரே is a stock half-line of the returning man (it opens Natrinai 21's order too), and the startled beasts are the land the chariot breaks into, not a sign.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowered scrub of the forest land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 3

486.reading: Why should she suffer hard pining, thinking without pause through the great dreary evening? So that the noble woman who could never have enough of embracing may see us, drive, charioteer, handling the reins with skill, your chariot yoked with bird-swift horses.
486.nuance: Line 3 (புல்லி ஆற்றாப் புரையோள்) may say she could never be sated with embracing, or that she cannot bear the absence even after embraces; the reading keeps the first. The last line repeats 481's horses but writes கலைமா (stag) where 481 has கலிமா (proud horse); as yoked to the chariot they are horses.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits through the evening and the man hurries home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 4

487.reading: This, surely, is the hour when those who are apart remember; so that the heart of her with close-set bangles may rejoice, drive the chariot, wise charioteer.
487.nuance: The season is pointed at (இது) rather than described: the man puts his own longing under a common law (those apart remember now) and makes her joy, not his, the reason to hurry. The praise of the charioteer's wit (மதியுடை) asks for skill as well as speed.

thinai_evidence.note: the hour of separated lovers' remembering, as the man returns

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 3

488.reading: The cloud-massed sky has begun to rain, and this is the hour my beloved thinks of me; yoke the good horses with spreading manes, mighty one, and drive the chariot so that her distress may end.
488.nuance: பெருவிறல் may address the charioteer (mighty one) or be the man's own title, 'the beloved of the man of great might'; the reading takes it as the address. The first rain is read as the moment she remembers him: he knows her mind by the season, so the weather itself is her summons.

thinai_evidence.note: the first rains of the season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; the order to yoke and drive is given in lines 3 and 4

489.reading: At the evening when mullai blooms on the soft land and swarms of striped bees with lovely wings crowd upon it, ply the fine-twisted strong reins and drive your long chariot of good horses fast, so that the girl of sorrowing heart may rejoice.
489.nuance: Evening and opening jasmine are the hour and flower of mullai, the hour her sorrow (பையுள்) is worst; he times his arrival to meet it. The bees crowding on the opening mullai could be read as the lover drawn to the woman, but the poem gives them no act of a person of the situation, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai blooming at evening on the soft land

thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; the order to drive is given in lines 4 and 5

490.reading: The rainy season has come to us, bringing back her lovely sweet speech; so, that the hard pining of her of choice bangles may end, drive fast the long chariot with its fine bells.
490.nuance: அம்தீம் கிளவி தான்தர can be read two ways: the rains bring her sweet words to his mind, or the season came as her sweet word had granted, the time she was told to wait for. Either way the season is tied to her voice, not to the king's business.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of the rainy season

links.note: Both returning men order the goad (Ainkurunuru: முள் இட்டு ஊர்மதி; Natrinai: தீண்டா வை முள் தீண்டி), and Natrinai's order opens with the same half-line ஏமதி வலவ தேரே that Ainkurunuru 485 uses.
links.teaches: Natrinai adds that this goad has never before touched these horses, which shows what Ainkurunuru's bare order assumes: the goad's sting was the convention for an urgency greater than any the charioteer had known.

links.note: Both set the king's war against the home feast in the man's mouth: the Kural lets the king win and the man feast at evening with his wife; Ainkurunuru says one more day with the victorious king would be an age.
links.teaches: The Kural states the two duties as a calm pair of wishes, while the Sangam poem shows the strain inside that balance, since the king's victory is honoured in a line and then a single day of further service is weighed as an aeon.

links.note: Natrinai 81's man pictures his wife eager to prepare a feast for his coming (விருந்து அயர் விருப்பொடு); Ainkurunuru 482's man calls himself the great feast she will have (பெருவிருந்து).
links.teaches: Read together they show the word virundhu turning in the return poems from the meal the wife prepares to the husband himself as the guest she receives, so his homecoming is framed as the household's rite of hospitality.

links.note: 483's man drives so the woman may get back her beauty (தன்னலம் பெறவே); in 200 the friend sees the bangles tighten and the brow grow lovely now that the lord of the golden chariot has come.
links.teaches: The same anthology gives the restoring of beauty first as the returning man's purpose and then as a fact the friend watches on the woman's body, so nalam regained is the agreed proof, in mullai and neythal alike, that a separation is over.

links.note: Akananuru 144's man imagines his wife saying he does not even remember her hair bare of mullai (கதுப்பும் உள்ளார்); Ainkurunuru 484's man says himself that they have stayed long, forgetting her (நீடினம் நேரிழை மறந்தே).
links.teaches: The charge of forgetting that the longer poem puts in the waiting wife's mouth, the short poem has the husband confess unprompted, so the return poems treat the man's own guilt over the delay as the counterpart of her reproach and the hurried drive as his answer to it.

links.note: In both the returning man drives through the rain-season scrub where deer run startled; Natrinai 242 follows one stag that will not leave but searches for its scattered doe.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru leaves the startled beasts as the land the chariot breaks through, while Natrinai singles out one stag seeking its mate, so the pair shows how the same stock scene becomes a mirror of the man's search for his wife only when one creature is given a lover's act.

links.note: Both praise the charioteer's wit with the same epithet (Ainkurunuru: மதியுடை வலவ; Kuruntokai: மதியுடை வல்லோய்): Ainkurunuru before the drive, Kuruntokai after it, for cutting a new road and bringing the chariot home today.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru asks for the charioteer's skill and Kuruntokai thanks him for having used it, so the two show the charioteer as more than a driver: the returning man credits him with the judgement that ends the wife's suffering.

links.note: In Akananuru 74 the friend comforts the heroine that the man, seeing the rain-washed scrub, will think of her and say 'drive, charioteer of the strong chariot'; Ainkurunuru 488 is a returning man saying just that as the rains begin.
links.teaches: Akananuru 74 shows the waiting wife doubting the comfort that he will remember her at the rains, and Ainkurunuru 488 gives the very order the friend predicted, so the decade supplies the man's side of a promise that the akam comforting formula only foretells.

links.note: Both bid the charioteer drive fast at the evening of the rains, when swarms of bees hum at the fragrant mullai; Akananuru 204 frames it with the Pandya's victory camp and ends on the woman's shoulders.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru gives the bee-and-mullai evening with only the girl's sorrowing heart for a goal, Akananuru wraps the same scene in a Pandya campaign, so the pair shows the king's war as an optional frame around a fixed core of season, hour and hurried drive.

source_issues: 482 line 2: வல்விரைத்து is probably a slip for வல்விரைந்து (very swiftly), the form used in the return poems (Akananuru 204 line 8); read as வல்விரைந்து.
486 line 5: கலைமாப் (stag) where 481 line 4 has the same half-line with கலிமாப் (proud horse); as yoked to the chariot the beasts are horses, and கலைமா is probably a variant or slip for கலிமா.
490 line 1: அம்தீம் கிளவி தான்தர is open to two readings (the rains bring back her sweet words, or came as her sweet word granted); the verse is marked uncertain.
